# Setting up {.unnumbered}

Work through this page **before Day 1**. It takes about half an hour, most of which is waiting for downloads. Doing it in advance means Session 1 starts with you writing model code rather than installing software.

You need four things: Julia, a code editor (we suggest VSCode), Quarto, and the course materials themselves. Follow the sections in order.

::: {.callout-tip}
## If you get stuck, try to keep installing the rest of the software and make a note of where you got stuck. 

A setup problem that has cost you thirty minutes alone could be a ten-minute fix in person. Note where you got stuck and move on. We will help you fix it on Day 1 if you can't get it working.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Never used a terminal? Start here

A terminal is a text-based window where you type commands to control your computer. Instead of clicking folders and icons with a mouse, you use your keyboard to tell the system what to do. Where a step below says "run this in a terminal", the grey box beneath it is the line to paste in, one line at a time, each followed by `Enter`.

To open one:

- **macOS**: press `Cmd`+`Space`, type `Terminal`, press `Enter`.
- **Windows**: click Start, type `PowerShell`, press `Enter`.
- **Linux**: your desktop's terminal application, usually `Ctrl`+`Alt`+`T`.

VSCode also has one built in, and it is the easier option once you reach [step 2](#install-vscode-and-the-julia-extension): open it with *Terminal* → *New Terminal*. It starts in whichever folder you have open, which is what steps 5 and 6 need. If you would rather not go hunting for a terminal application at all, do step 2 first and then come back here.
:::

## 1. Install Julia

Install Julia through **juliaup**, a small tool that manages Julia versions for you. It means you can update Julia later, or hold several versions side by side, without reinstalling anything.

On **Windows**, you can do this without a terminal. Open the **Microsoft Store** app, search for **Julia**, and click *Get*. That installs juliaup.

You can also use the [manual download](https://julialang.org/downloads/manual-downloads/) to install juliaup if you would rather follow a link and use a GUI-based installer.

If you prefer a command, this does exactly the same job:

```bash
winget install --name Julia --id 9NJNWW8PVKMN -e -s msstore
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## If the winget command fails

If the winget command fails with a certificate error that starts with something like "Failed when opening source(s).... The server certificate did not match any of the expected values." You can try the following instead:

- Run in PowerShell as Administrator and enable the certificate bypass:
```bash
winget settings --enable BypassCertificatePinningForMicrosoftStore
```

- Now you can run thecommand to install Julia:
```bash
winget install --id 9NJNWW8PVKMN --exact --source msstore
```

- Run the following command to restore the security setting afterwards:
```bash
winget settings --disable BypassCertificatePinningForMicrosoftStore
```
:::


On **macOS or Linux**, you could try the manual download and install as well, or this one line in a terminal:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

It asks you to confirm where it will install things; press `Enter` to accept the defaults.

Then close and reopen your terminal, and install the version this course is built and tested against. These two lines are typed, on every platform including Windows:

```bash
juliaup add 1.12.5
juliaup default 1.12.5
```

Check that it worked by typing `julia`:

```bash
$ julia
               _
   _       _ _(_)_     |  Documentation: https://docs.julialang.org
  (_)     | (_) (_)    |
   _ _   _| |_  __ _   |  Type "?" for help, "]?" for Pkg help.
  | | | | | | |/ _` |  |
  | | |_| | | | (_| |  |  Version 1.12.5
 _/ |\__'_|_|_|\__'_|  |
|__/                   |

julia>
```

It must read exactly `1.12.5`, patch version included. The course's `Manifest.toml` records the Julia version everything was resolved and tested against, and Quarto refuses to run a document when the Julia you started differs from it, so a newer patch release stops worksheets rendering with a `Julia version mismatch` error. This is why the commands above name the full version rather than the `1.12` channel, which would follow whichever patch is newest. That prompt is the Julia **REPL**. Leave it with `exit()` or `Ctrl-D`.

If `julia` is not found, see [Julia is not found](#julia-is-not-found) below.

## 2. Install VSCode and the Julia extension

Download Visual Studio Code from [code.visualstudio.com/download](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and install it.

Then install the Julia extension: open the Extensions panel with `Cmd`+`Shift`+`X` (macOS) or `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`X` (Windows and Linux), search for **Julia** (Julia Language Support), and click *Install*.

Restart VSCode afterwards. To confirm the extension works, open the command palette with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, run **Julia: Start REPL**, and check that a `julia>` prompt appears in the panel at the bottom.

If the extension cannot find Julia, see [VSCode cannot find Julia](#vscode-cannot-find-julia) below.

::: {.callout-note}
## The Revise message when the REPL starts

When you start the Julia REPL in VSCode, you may see the following setup message:

> Julia is configured to load Revise when the REPL starts, but Revise is not installed.

[Revise.jl](https://timholy.github.io/Revise.jl/stable/) lets Julia pick up edits to the source of a package you have already loaded, without restarting the REPL. However, nothing in this course edits package source, so you do not need it.

You can leave the message and close it each time it appears, or stop VSCode looking for Revise each time you start the REPL:

1. Open the settings with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`,`.
2. Search for `julia.useRevise`, shown as *Julia › Execution: Use Revise*.
3. Clear the checkbox.
4. Stop the Julia REPL and start it again.
:::

## 3. Install Quarto

The chapters and worksheets are Quarto documents. You need both the Quarto program and its VSCode extension: the extension is what runs a single code cell while you read, and the program is what turns a finished worksheet into an HTML report.

1. Download and install Quarto 1.9 or newer from [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/).
2. In VSCode, install the **Quarto** extension the same way you installed the Julia one.

Confirm the program is on your path (if you had your terminal open when you installed Quarto, you may need to close and reopen it):

```bash
quarto --version
```

## 4. Get the course materials

If you use **git**:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/epirecipes/modeling-epidemics-julia.git
cd modeling-epidemics-julia
```

If you do not use git, open [the repository](https://github.com/epirecipes/modeling-epidemics-julia), choose *Code* then *Download ZIP*, and unzip it somewhere you can find again.

Then open that folder in VSCode with *File* → *Open Folder*. Open the folder itself (e.g., `modeling-epidemics-julia-main`), not an individual file. Julia and Quarto both need to know which project you are working in, and VSCode tells them by which folder is open. Be sure you are opening the specific project folder, rather than your general `Downloads` folder.

## 5. Install the course packages

From the top of the folder you just opened, run the following command in a terminal (NOT the Julia REPL):

```bash
julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
```

This command activates the project in the current directory and installs all course dependencies. It is the longest setup step, so a stable internet connection is recommended. Allow several minutes for the packages to download and precompile.

::: {.callout-note}
## What `--project=.` means

It activates the Julia project in the current directory. In this case, it tells Julia to use the set of packages declared in this folder. If you forget it, Julia falls back to your personal default set, if the course packages are not there, loading a package like `using CairoMakie` can fail (which is the most common problem people hit). See [a package seems to be missing](#a-package-seems-to-be-missing).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What `-e '...'` means

It evaluates the enclosed Julia code when we run the command from the terminal. If we are in the REPL, we would just type whatever we want to evaluate after the `julia>` prompt.
:::

## 6. Check that it worked

Run this from the terminal. You can open a new terminal from inside VSCode by clicking *Terminal* → *+*. The enclosed Julia code (in single quotes) loads the two packages the first worksheet needs, builds and displays a figure.

```bash
julia --project=. -e '
using CairoMakie, StableRNGs
println("Julia version: ", VERSION)
fig = Figure(size = (400, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1])
xs = 0:0.05:6
lines!(ax, xs, exp.(-xs))
display(fig)
println("CairoMakie and StableRNGs load, and a figure builds.")
println("Setup complete.")'
```

Or, if you prefer to run it in the REPL, you can open the Julia REPL as before, `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P` → *Julia: Start REPL*. 

```julia
using CairoMakie, StableRNGs
println("Julia version: ", VERSION)
fig = Figure(size = (400, 300));
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]);
xs = 0:0.05:6;
lines!(ax, xs, exp.(-xs));
display(fig);
```

You should see your Julia version and the following figure:

```{julia}
#| output: true
#| echo: false
using CairoMakie, StableRNGs
fig = Figure(size = (400, 300));
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]);
xs = 0:0.05:6;
lines!(ax, xs, exp.(-xs));
display(fig);
```

Once this passes, you are ready. Everything below is either troubleshooting or optional.

## 7. Running code while you follow along

You will meet the course material in three forms, and each is run differently.

**Worksheets and chapters** are Quarto documents, made of prose with code cells. Put the cursor inside a cell and press `Shift`+`Enter` to run that cell. The Julia REPL opens (if it is not already running), and the whole cell is run there. Printed output appears in the REPL, and figures are shown in the plot pane.

To turn a finished worksheet into a PDF or HTML report, you can render it from the command line:

```bash
quarto render worksheets/prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd --to html
```

Or using VScode shortcut: `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P` → *Quarto: Render*, and select the document type (e.g., `PDF`).

**Your own scripts:** If you create a plain julia file (`.jl` file), you can put the cursor on a line and press `Shift`+`Enter` to send just that line to the REPL. To run several lines together, fence them between `#%%` markers and press `Alt/Option`+`Enter` anywhere inside the block:

```julia
#%%
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
#%%
```

Because `#` starts a comment in Julia, you can label a block by writing after the marker (i.e., `#%% force of infection`).

**The REPL itself** can be used for short questions that may not need to be saved on a script: what a function takes, whether a package is installed, what a value is. It has three modes beyond the ordinary `julia>` prompt. Type the character at an empty prompt to enter one, and `Backspace` to leave:

| Key | Mode | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `?` | help | you want a function's arguments — `?expm1` |
| `]` | package | a package seems missing — `]st` also names the active project |
| `;` | shell | you need `ls` or `git status` without leaving Julia |

## If something goes wrong

### VSCode cannot find Julia

If `julia` works in a terminal but VSCode reports that it cannot find it, tell the extension where to look. First get the path:

```bash
which julia     # macOS and Linux
where julia     # Windows
```

Then open VSCode's settings with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`,`, search for **Julia Executable Path**, and paste the result in.

### Julia is not found

If your shell does not know where Julia was installed, the usual cause is that the shell was open while Julia was installed, so close it and open a new terminal.

If that doesn't work, on macOS or Linux, add juliaup's directory to your path by putting this line in `~/.zshrc` (or `~/.bashrc` if you use bash — `echo $SHELL` tells you which):

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.juliaup/bin:$PATH"
```

### A package seems to be missing

If `using CairoMakie` fails with a message about the package not being found, Julia is almost certainly running outside the course project.

Check which project is active: at the Julia prompt, press `]` to enter package mode. The prompt changes to show the active project's name, which should be `(EpiModelingCourse)`. If it shows `(@v1.12)` instead, you are in your personal default environment. Press `Backspace` to leave package mode, quit with `exit()`, and start Julia again with `--project=.` from the top of the course folder.

## Optional extras

**Recommended font.** The course writes parameters as `β`, `γ` and `λ` so the code matches the equations. Most fonts show these, but [JuliaMono](https://juliamono.netlify.app/download/) is designed for Julia and covers every symbol the course uses. Install it, then open VSCode's settings ( `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`,`) and in *Editor: Font Family* add `JuliaMono` at the beginning of the list.

**Typing Greek letters.** You do not need that font to type the symbols. At any Julia prompt, and in `.jl` files, type a backslash, the name, then `Tab`: `\beta`+`Tab` gives `β`. 

However, inside a Quarto `.qmd` file the Tab completition may not work.For those, install the **Unicode Latex** extension: open the Extensions panel, search for `unicode-latex`, and install the one published by Omer Sheikh. Its symbol names are generated from Julia's own REPL completions, so they are the names this course uses. To insert a character, open the command palette with `Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Shift`+`P`, type `unicode`, choose **Unicode: Insert Math Symbol**, type the symbol's name, and press `Enter`. 

Every worksheet also opens with a table of the symbols it uses, ready to copy.

**The interactive notebooks.** Every unit also comes as a Pluto notebook with sliders, linked at the end of its chapter. Step 5 already installed Pluto, so starting it is one line:

```bash
julia --project=. -e 'using Pluto; Pluto.run()'
```

It opens in your browser. Use *Open a notebook* and give it a path such as `notebooks/chapters/01-foundations.jl`.

A Pluto notebook is not a script that runs top to bottom. Its cells form a network: change one, and every cell that depends on it re-runs by itself. To stop Pluto, press `Ctrl`+`C` in the terminal where it is running.

**A second package set.** One unit, parameter estimation, needs a package that conflicts with the rest of the course, so it has an environment of its own. It is OK to skip this unless and until you work through that chapter:

```bash
julia --project=environments/ch09 -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
```
